Applied Language Models

RAG vs. LoRA Fine-Tuning

for Course-Specific Question Answering

Tamar Telele · Applied Language Models · Dr. Barak Or

When does retrieval beat fine-tuning — and why?

Two ways to teach a model a new domain.
RAG looks the answer up. LoRA learns it into its weights.

They are usually compared as rivals. We tested them as collaborators.

One corpus · one frozen base model · one test set, opened once

The whole system on one slide

Everything below the dashed line runs on the same frozen flan-t5-base — every difference is caused by method, not model size. “Top-3” = the three most relevant chunks retrieved per question and placed in the prompt.
1

Building the dataset

From 9 PDFs to 1,130 QA pairs

  • Page-level extraction keeps file + page for every text span — free ground truth, zero manual labelling
  • Gemini generates QA pairs under a strict grounding instruction and structured JSON output
  • Typed mix on purpose: 54.4% factual · 34.8% conceptual · 10.8% comparative
A dataset of only “what is X?” cannot tell RAG and LoRA apart — both handle definitions well.

Three filters, cheapest first

  • 1 · Heuristics — length, degenerate answers, leakage phrases, near-duplicates
  • 2 · LLM-as-a-Judge — 4 criteria, temp 0.0
  • 3 · Sample audit — manual review + ChatGPT corrections
Accept only if mean ≥ 4.0 AND groundedness ≥ 4 separately — 89.1% passed, 1,130 pairs remain.
2

Building the RAG pipeline

Chunk size is a decision, not a default

  • sentence 50 tok, 10 overlap → 1,407 chunks
  • paragraph 300 tok, 50 overlap → 208 chunks
  • slide 500 tok, 75 overlap → 125 chunks
  • Same splitter (RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter) — only size & overlap move
Overlap = shared tokens between consecutive chunks, so a sentence cut at a boundary still appears whole in one of them. An 11× spread in chunk count — which size retrieves best is an empirical question.

The pretrained embedding space already captures real semantics

This is an off-the-shelf frozen encoder (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) — we never trained it, it arrived pretrained. Classical ML, Intro and Deep Learning Principles overlap (shared vocabulary) · Deep Reinforcement Learning stands apart, sharing almost no vocabulary with the rest.

…but the sharpest clusters did not win

  • Paragraph-level looks best in t-SNE — the clusters are visibly cleanest
  • Sentence-level won every single retrieval configuration
  • t-SNE asks: is this chunk identifiable?  Retrieval asks: does it answer the question?
A 50-token window holds one fact with no noise. That is what a specific question matches.

Retrieval grid — 3 chunk sizes × 3 methods

ConfigurationMRRHit@1Hit@3
sentence + Hybrid0.7060.5650.847
sentence + Dense0.6870.5470.812
sentence + BM250.6570.5290.771
paragraph + Hybrid0.6700.5060.835
slide + Hybrid0.6200.4940.724
Fusion combines each retriever's top-50 candidates; only the final top-3 go to the reader. Hybrid wins every chunk size, sentence wins every method. Selected on MRR, not Hit@3.

Tuning α, and knowing when to stay quiet

  • α = 0.7 — 70% Dense, 30% BM25  →  MRR 0.717 · Hit@3 0.841
  • Dense generalises across paraphrase; BM25 rescues exact technical terms
  • Guardrail calibrated to 0.330 → 100% balanced accuracy
  • In-scope p05 = 0.462 vs out-of-scope p95 = 0.294 — a clean 0.168 margin
An assistant that invents an answer to an off-syllabus question is worse than useless.
3

LoRA fine-tuning

Searching for the best LoRA settings

  • Coordinate search: tune one factor at a time
  • But α and r interact — the adapter scales by α/r
  • So the full r×α grid was measured, one cell at a time
  • Winner: word · r=8 · α=32 · dropout 0.05
r=16 scored worse than r=8 despite twice the parameters — a sign of overfitting to the small training set.

The final adapter

  • ROUGE-L 0.2612 — best of all 16 runs
  • 884,736 trainable params = 0.36% of the model
  • 6 MB adapter vs 990 MB base
  • Training and validation loss track together — no overfitting
One frozen base can serve many tasks, each swapping in its own small adapter.
4

Results

Test set — opened exactly once

SystemROUGE-LBLEULatency
Baseline (zero-shot)0.1680.0150.67 s
RAG0.3890.2040.75 s
LoRA0.2730.0571.10 s
Hybrid (RAG + LoRA)0.4440.2381.05 s
2.6× ROUGE-L and 15.9× BLEU over the floor. Hybrid exceeds both parts — so they carry different signal.

Where Hybrid wins most

  • Factual  +0.053 over RAG
  • Conceptual  +0.035 over RAG
  • Comparative  +0.114 over RAG
Comparison needs several facts and a learned way to phrase them. Neither mechanism does that alone.

The bottleneck is the reader, not the index

Three independent measurements, one conclusion: better embeddings would return little — a better reader would return a great deal.
5

Errors and hallucination

Hallucination needs a semantic test

  • Word overlap cannot detect a fabricated fact
  • DeBERTa-v3 NLI: reference = premise, each claim = hypothesis
  • Flagged only on contradiction > 0.70
  • Paraphrase and vagueness are never punished
That distinction — contradicting vs merely differing — is what no overlap metric can make.

Retrieval is what suppresses fabrication

SystemHallucinationROUGE-L
LoRA (no retrieval)14.3%0.273
RAG (retrieval)11.9%0.389
Hybrid (retrieval)11.9%0.444
LoRA invented: TensorFlow → UC Berkeley · PyTorch → Carnegie Mellon. Both fluent, both false, contradiction 1.000.

Hallucination ≠ a low score

Flat across quartiles. A model can paraphrase correctly and still fabricate — or score well and still be false.

What is the difference between RAG and LoRA fine-tuning?
RAGI don't have enough information in the course material

Not in the slides → RAG and Hybrid abstain. LoRA has no guardrail, so it answers anyway.

High confidence. Wrong answer.

Q: What is the function of convolutional layers in a CNN?   Reference: They extract features from the input image.
Retrieved at similarity 0.997 · 0.964 · 0.896 — all from the correct PDF, all about CNNs.
RAGvisualizing which parts of an image activate the neurons in a CNN
Hybridthe first convolutional layer specifies the input shape (28×28×1) and uses 32 filters of size 3×3
Both sentences are about convolutional layers. Neither answers the question — and Hit@k records this as a success.

What I would fix next

Limitations

  • Reference answers were graded automatically — the grading itself isn't perfect
  • Our reader model is fairly small, and it's the main limit on quality
  • We compared chunk sizes, not different chunking methods

Future work

  • Try a bigger reader model — the most likely source of improvement
  • Regenerate the question set with a stronger model
  • Train LoRA together with retrieval, instead of separately
  • Add a re-ranking step after retrieval, before answering

Retrieval and fine-tuning are complementary, not competing

  • Hybrid wins every metric because each mechanism supplies what the other lacks
  • Retrieval suppresses fabrication — 14.3% → 11.9%, adapter unchanged
  • The reader is the ceiling — not the retriever
  • Hallucination is its own axis — one score cannot measure both
All of it on one frozen checkpoint — which is what makes the numbers mean anything.
